task_1.title: Align flask.json.loads typing with bytes input support
task_1.description: The library updates the public type signature of JSON deserialization so `flask.json.loads` explicitly accepts both text and byte input, matching the underlying Python JSON API and preventing incorrect static typing errors for valid byte-based usage.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that `flask.json.loads` is documented and typed as accepting both JSON text and JSON bytes so valid byte-based deserialization is treated as supported usage.

expectation.grounded: The public signature for `flask.json.loads` should accept `str` and `bytes` for its first argument, aligning the Flask helper with the accepted input contract of Python's `json.loads`. Code that passes byte content to `flask.json.loads` should be treated as valid by type-aware tooling, while existing string input support remains unchanged.
expectation.conceptual: JSON deserialization through Flask should support the same common input forms users expect from Python's JSON loader. Applications providing either text or raw byte payloads should be able to use the same API without being told that byte input is unsupported.

constraints.grounded: Do not narrow or alter existing support for string input to `flask.json.loads`. Preserve the API's deserialization role and optional parameters while expanding the accepted input annotation to include bytes only as an additional supported input form.
constraints.conceptual: This update should broaden the declared input contract without changing how existing callers use the API or introducing unrelated behavior changes.

behavior: `flask.json.loads` declares its first argument as accepting both `str` and `bytes`.
Passing byte content to `flask.json.loads` is part of the supported public API contract rather than a type-level incompatibility.
Passing string content to `flask.json.loads` remains supported with no change to the API's deserialization purpose.
acceptance_criteria: When application code passes a `bytes` JSON payload to `flask.json.loads`, the library's public API contract should recognize that input as valid.
When application code passes a `str` JSON payload to `flask.json.loads`, it should remain valid and unaffected by this update.
The accepted input types for `flask.json.loads` should stay aligned with the corresponding Python JSON deserialization API for text and byte input.

task_2.title: Allow `flask run` certificate and key options in either order
task_2.description: Flask 2.1.2 fixes `flask run` HTTPS option handling so a certificate file and key file are accepted regardless of whether `--cert` or `--key` is written first, preventing a false CLI validation failure for valid input.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that `flask run` accepts HTTPS certificate and key arguments when both are provided, regardless of whether `--cert` or `--key` appears first, instead of rejecting a valid configuration based only on option order.

expectation.grounded: On the `flask run` CLI, when `--cert` and `--key` are both provided with file values, the command should parse them as one HTTPS configuration whether `--cert` precedes `--key` or `--key` precedes `--cert`. Reversed ordering must not cause a parameter validation failure, while incomplete usage such as supplying `--key` without a corresponding `--cert` should remain invalid.
expectation.conceptual: Users should be able to start the development server with HTTPS by passing both the certificate and private key options in any order. The CLI should reject only genuinely incomplete TLS configuration, not a different ordering of otherwise valid arguments.

constraints.grounded: Do not change the public meaning of `flask run`, `--cert`, or `--key` beyond making option order irrelevant for a valid certificate/key pair. The command must continue to require a complete file-based HTTPS configuration and must not change unrelated CLI behavior.
constraints.conceptual: Keep the fix narrowly scoped to argument ordering. Existing HTTPS configuration rules should stay the same, and unrelated command behavior should not change.

behavior: `flask run` accepts `--cert` and `--key` in either order when both are present with file arguments.
Providing `--key` before `--cert` no longer triggers an order-dependent CLI validation error.
Supplying an incomplete key-only HTTPS configuration remains invalid command usage.
acceptance_criteria: When a user runs `flask run` with both a certificate file and a key file, the command should accept the configuration whether `--cert` appears before `--key` or after it.
When a user provides `--key` first and then `--cert`, the command should treat the two options as one valid HTTPS configuration instead of failing during argument parsing.
When a user provides a key file without the required certificate file, the command should still reject the configuration as invalid.
